lines.text: The Lists were simpler than the Shoot. Two champions, one ring of sand, and the first to yield or fall, lost.
Lord Fane, of the southern march! Ember! Five rings!
And against him, Wren of Greyhollow, under the Princess's name. A commoner, the herald said, of three rings. He sounded embarrassed for her.
I'll be gentle, girl. It would be bad manners to burn a lady in front of the King.
He wasn't gentle. Fire came off his sword in sheets. Wren ran, and shot, and ran again, and every arrow burned to ash before it reached him.
Then, in the middle of a swing, his ring flickered.
It went pale, like a candle at the end of a long night. And the fire on his blade went out with it.
No. No, not now! Not here!
Wren didn't stop to ask what was wrong. Her first arrow took the sword out of his hand. Her second pinned his cloak to the sand.
Nobody knew whether to cheer. Then a baker in the Lowmarket stand threw Wren a loaf, and she caught it on the point of an arrow, and the Lowmarket decided to cheer anyway.
In the royal box, the Grand Measurer was turning a cup of wine in his fingers. He did not look surprised.
He saw me watching, and raised his cup to me. Hask had done that once, across my square. I hadn't liked it then, either.
That evening, Tamsin slipped into Wren's tent with her hood up. Wren was still furious.
I didn't beat him. Something left him. I want to know what.
The Order lends aether to loyal houses, poured into glass. As long as a house stays loyal, its glass stays full.
And when it stops being loyal?
Then the Order stops pouring.
I thought of Penhallow in the bathhouse steam, his ring flickering like a candle in a draught. Rings don't flicker. Not unless they were never yours.
That payment I told you about, my lord. Every quarter-day, to a house with no name. I think I know the house now. It has seven rings over the door.
And last week, Lord Fane stood up in the King's council and spoke against the Order's tithe.
So he wasn't beaten. He was punished. In front of forty thousand people.
Later that night, a lord came to our tent, and asked for Sir Oswin by his old title, the one the King had taken away.
Sir Oswin Hale, of the King's Third Company. Still squeamish about fire, Hale?
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter eighty-seven, coming soon.
